Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
The world is a dangerous place
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

vignette: Eduardo was sixty-two when the sexual assault occurred during a summer visit to his sister's house in Arizona. He had come to believe that the danger was tied to the exact temperature the guest room's mattress held against his back that night. What frightened him most was the specific, cool weight pressing against his skin, a tactile mark that never fully lifted. In the weeks that followed, the memory of the event did not settle into old history; it felt like it was happening right now. When the air in any room matched that guest room's chill, or when a related person stepped into his line of sight, the frightening moment would force its way into his mind, unbidden and unfiltered. He would stand perfectly still, his breath catching, certain that the past had arrived again. The memories were very clear and detailed, down to the pattern of the wallpaper and the precise pressure against his ribs. He was certain that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, a deep, unyielding vulnerability remaining in his torso. Alongside this physical reckoning, he felt dirty and contaminated, as if the violation had left something clinging to his skin and clothes. He began washing more often, not because he was ill, but because the sensation of impurity persisted regardless of cleanliness. The world, he decided, was a dangerous place, and his body was no longer the reliable vessel it had once been. These appraisals coexisted in his daily attention; one did not give rise to the other. Now sixty-seven, Eduardo continued his work as a prosecutor, a role that required him to navigate both familiar corridors and shifting legal landscapes. He worked primarily in a historic courthouse with heavy oak doors and polished marble, spaces that felt manageable because he knew their layout. When he traveled to depose witnesses or attend hearings in unfamiliar buildings, however, he would pause at the threshold, scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room. He could not assess the danger of a space until he located every way out. He noticed weapons constantly, keeping a careful eye on the glass water pitcher on a conference table, the heavy brass letter opener on the clerk's desk, or the metal scissors left on a witness stand. He avoided going to unfamiliar places; the inability to assess the danger remained his own certainty. Over months, this scanning became a quiet, unshaken ritual. He would measure doorways, test door handles, and keep his jacket close, his hands resting against the fabric. Children present became a particular trigger; their sudden movements and proximity stirred a quiet alarm, even though his grandchildren were entirely harmless. He would step back, adjusting his cuffs, certain that the world's unpredictability extended to every room. His wife's passing had left him without the person who had once navigated the outside world alongside him, and his avoidance of unfamiliar spaces meant he attended fewer family gatherings, preferring the familiar quiet of his home. With a PCL-5 score of 50, his symptoms settled into a steady rhythm. What finally brought him to seek help was the unrelenting force of his memories. They no longer waited for temperature shifts or familiar faces to surface; they invaded his lunch breaks and his courtroom preparations with startling clarity. He was hoping, he said, to find a way to live with the cool weight on his skin and the ever-present awareness of his vulnerable body, without letting the fear dictate every door he chose to open.
